newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain unions, employers bicker over labour reform.
newsitem.headline: Spain unions, employers bicker over labour reform.

text.p: Spanish unions and employers will meet on Friday to continue talks on labour market reform in an increasingly tense atmosphere which might make the government intervene.
So far the two parties seem to disagree about everything -- even about how much progress has been made in the talks -- and time is running out.
They have until March to reach a deal or the government will step in, the Secretary General for Employment Manuel Pimentel said on Thursday.
"There's no concrete time limit for (the government) to enter negotiations, but by around the beginning of March we'd expect to see something from the talks," Pimentel told Reuters.
Spain wants negotiated measures to help to cut a 13.82 percent unemployment rate, Europe's highest, and reduce the risk of strike action.
But unions complained on Wednesday that the talks were stuck, with employers still failing to suggest acceptable measures to tackle the problem.
"I have to say that negotiations are going badly...Employers are still thinking in terms of the temporary and the precarious," Antonio Gutierrez, head of leading union CCOO, told a labour seminar.
His opposite number at the employers association CEOE disagreed that the talks were blocked. But he could not guarantee the two sides would reach a compromise.

"I can't say there will be an agreement, but I do think that the talks are not suspended or blocked, but rather that they are at a complex and difficult time, which this kind of agreement always passes," Jose Maria Cuevas said.
Employers are looking for a structural reform of the labour market, and expressed concern at what they described as "miracle recipes" from the unions, such as job-sharing schemes.
Their main bug-bear is high dismissal costs for workers on permanent contracts, which they say makes employers reluctant to take on employees long-term.
Currently bosses have to pay redundant workers 20 days' pay for each year they have been employed if no economic grounds for dismissal have been cited.
A partial reform by the previous Socialist government in 1994 introduced special contracts for apprenticeships, aiming to boost jobs for the young, and made hiring temporary employees easier.

But it left aside the issue of high dismissal costs for permanent workers. Critics say the reform simply widened the divide between permanent and temporary workers, and increased insecurity for some people. One in three Spanish employees has a temporary contract.
A Labour Ministry survey found that over 96 percent of new jobs created in 1996 were temporary, and half of those were on contracts lasting less than a month.
The government recognises the problem is to tackle unemployment for younger people, who suffer most from it.
But it seems increasingly likely that the administration will have to present a concrete plan of its own, despite tentatively optimistic statements.
"We've set out some very wide fields for discussion, including things such as job stability. We think that both sides are still prepared to negotiate, and that's the important thing," Pimentel said.
